transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-02-07
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Omar Salazar (Redwood SE), Jared Liu (Solaris Platform), Priya Nair (Solaris Security), Marco Ruiz (Solaris Cloud)

Summary: Solaris Labs is evaluating Redwood Private for a multi-region deployment that must satisfy EU data residency and low-latency US EU hops for certain workloads. They're weighing transit gateway peering vs PrivateLink style endpoints and are concerned about egress inspection, certificate/BYOK rotation, and network hairpins for cross-region inference.\n
Topics:
- VPC peering vs PrivateLink/private endpoints tradeoffs
- Transit gateway chaining and MWAA (mist-transcribed) implications
- Multi-region data residency and model pinning by region
- Egress inspection and TLS termination (proxy vs mTLS)
- Dedicated vs Private cost and capacity model

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey all, thanks for jumping on. Quick round robin, then we'll dive into the network constraints. Um, Omar and I are from Redwood, I'm Maya AE and Omar is our solutions engineer.
[00:10] Jared Liu: Hey team, Jared here. We're the platform folks, I'll be the main point on network.
[00:13] Priya Nair: Priya from security. We'll look at compliance, egress inspection and key management.
[00:17] Marco Ruiz: Marco, cloud architect. I'll own the cloud topology and transit gateway bits.
[00:21] Omar Salazar: Great, thanks. Quick agenda: understand Solaris current topology, latency SLOs, region constraints, then walk tradeoffs between peering, private endpoints, and Private deployment options.
[00:30] Jared Liu: Broadly we run in AWS and GCP, mainly aws eu-west-1 and us-east-1, with pockets in asia-southeast-1 for experiments. We have a transit-gw-based hub and spoke, lots of VPCs attached.
[00:38] Maya Chen: Are you using TGW for cross-account attachments or a mix of VPC peering?
[00:41] Marco Ruiz: Mostly TGW. A few older services still use peering, but new ones go through TGW. The wrinkle: our security team wants to do egress inspection in eu-west-1 before any traffic leaves EU.
[00:49] Priya Nair: Correct. For any PII or regulated inference, traffic must be inspected by our egress proxy in-region. We also need audit logs for every call.
[00:56] Omar Salazar: Understood. One clarifying thing: when you say 'inspection', are you expecting TLS termination at the egress proxy, or mTLS hop-to-hop with TLS origination kept in Redwood?
[01:04] Priya Nair: Ideally we want TLS terminated at our proxy for DLP inspection. We can do mTLS if required, but that'll need cert rotation automation.
[01:12] Maya Chen: That's helpful. Quick note on Redwood Private: our private deployment supports a customer-managed control plane inside your VPCs or connected via a private control plane option, so you can keep network flow entirely within your peering or private endpoints. For TLS, we support mTLS and can also integrate with your KMS/HSM for BYOK.
[01:30] Marco Ruiz: When you say private endpoints, is that equivalent to AWS PrivateLink or something you host inside our VPCs?
[01:36] Omar Salazar: Good question. We have two patterns. One is PrivateLink-style ENI-based private endpoints in your VPC that hit Redwood service nodes in the same region. The other is a full Private deployment where Redwood's runtime is provisioned into your account or VPC and the control plane is either customer-managed or connected via a private peering link.
[01:51] Jared Liu: If we go with private endpoints, how do we handle cross-region calls? For example, EU model pinned to eu-west-1 but some requests may be originated in us-east-1 and need low latency.
[02:00] Omar Salazar: Two options: route requests to region-local endpoints only — clients in us-east-1 would hit the us-east-1 endpoint, which has a model variant or same model replicated in that region; or we allow cross-region routing over your TGW with IPSEC/peering, but that introduces egress and latency.
[02:12] Priya Nair: We can't move EU resident data to US unless it's anonymized; regulators require the data to stay in EU for certain customers.
[02:18] Maya Chen: We support model pinning by region so you can configure policies that keep inference for EU accounts restricted to eu-west-1. For shared or anonymized traffic you can allow cross-region fallback.
[02:27] Marco Ruiz: Any performance hit for model replication across regions? We worry about token-latency and cold-starts.
[02:33] Omar Salazar: Replicating warmed model VMs adds cost but removes cold-start latency. We use a continuous batching runtime and warm pools. There's a tradeoff: higher idle capacity in additional regions vs occasional cross-region hops. We can show benchmarks but ballpark is <15ms per token variance when running warm pools in the same region vs cross-region which can add 50-150ms depending on route.
[02:51] Jared Liu: Ok. For our high-throughput workloads, we need predictable throughput with autoscaling, and we'd like guardrails to avoid runaway cost during traffic spikes.
[02:58] Maya Chen: Dedicated capacity is the middle-ground — reserved GPU pools that you control. Private gives you the same guarantees but inside your network. We can wire autoscale policies and burst capacity limits; also provide quotas and throttles at token-level per API key.
[03:10] Marco Ruiz: Let's talk about Transit GW specifics. We have shared-services VPC where the egress inspection lives — if the Redwood nodes are in another account/region, how do we avoid hairpinning?
[03:19] Omar Salazar: Hairpinning happens when traffic goes out to Redwood's region then back through your TGW for inspection. To avoid that, we can either deploy Redwood runtime in the same region/VPC as your inspection proxy or use PrivateLink endpoints in-region so that calls never egress to the internet.
[03:30] Priya Nair: We also need full request/response audit logs, immutable, and ideally forwarded to our SIEM. Does Redwood ship those logs to our S3 or can we pull them via private ingestion?
[03:39] Maya Chen: Yes — logs can be forwarded to customer-managed S3 buckets or to your SIEM via our private ingestion connector. For Private deployments, logs never traverse public internet and are written locally first. We'll need an IAM role from your side to push to the bucket.
[03:50] Marco Ruiz: BYOK — we want to use our HSM for all key operations including model encryption and TLS cert signing. Is that supported?
[03:56] Omar Salazar: We support BYOK for data-at-rest encryption and KMS integration for key wrapping. For mTLS certs, you can bring certs and we support vault-based rotation hooks. Full HSM signing flows depend on your provider but we can integrate via standard PKCS#11 or cloud KMS APIs.
[04:10] Jared Liu: What's the control plane topology? We need to know if Redwood needs outbound control plane connectivity or if everything can be managed inside our VPC without public egress.
[04:18] Maya Chen: There are two control plane patterns. Hosted has control plane in Redwood cloud and requires private peering or egress. Private has a customer-managed control plane that runs in your VPC and doesn't require public egress. There's also a hybrid where control plane signals are proxied over an encrypted channel to Redwood's management plane but the data plane stays local. We can provide both depending on compliance.
[04:36] Priya Nair: For us, the sweet spot is customer-managed control plane in-region with private endpoints and audit logging to our S3. We want minimal egress.
[04:44] Marco Ruiz: Any special network ACLs or ports we need to allow for the runtime nodes?
[04:48] Omar Salazar: Standard: outbound HTTPS to your S3 and KMS endpoints if you use cloud KMS; for inter-node communication we use a small set of TCP ports (we'll share exact port list). If you use PrivateLink, ports are over ENI and don't require internet NAT. We'll provide a config template.
[05:00] Maya Chen: I'll attach the runbook and the port matrix after this call.
[05:03] Jared Liu: Good. Another ask: we run some on-prem VMware clusters for low-latency inference near edge devices. Can Redwood Private be deployed into on-prem or connected via Direct Connect/ExpressRoute?
[05:12] Omar Salazar: Yes. We have an on-prem package that can run in air-gapped or on-prem clusters and integrate via Direct Connect/ExpressRoute. The setup needs network eBPF tuning and some kernel modules, but we have docs and an engineering workshop we can schedule.
[05:25] Marco Ruiz: Sounds promising. What about rate limiting at the network perimeter? We want to ensure abusive requests don't saturate our egress inspection box.
[05:32] Maya Chen: We provide per-key throttles, per-route quotas, and can front Redwood nodes with your ALB/NLB so you can apply network-level protections before traffic hits the runtime. Also our Optimize product suggests batching thresholds to keep token costs down while preserving latency SLOs.
[05:45] Priya Nair: For compliance we need a SOC2 attestation and penetration test reports. Do you have those?
[05:50] Maya Chen: Yes, we have SOC2 Type II and ISO artifacts; I'll share the security pack. For Private customers we also supply deployment hardening checklists and an optional on-site pen test add-on we can arrange.
[05:58] Jared Liu: One more tricky bit — we have customers in Germany who require data residency in eu-central-1 specifically. Do you support region-pin to a very specific region per customer account?
[06:07] Omar Salazar: We do. Our routing policy supports per-tenant region pinning and per-route model versions. You can lock a tenant to eu-central-1 and have model variants available only in that region.
[06:15] Marco Ruiz: Let's drill into the PrivateLink vs TGW peering cost differences — we've seen PrivateLink endpoints incur hourly ENI/NLB costs per AZ. TGW is more flexible but you still have inter-region data transfer fees.
[06:25] Maya Chen: Right. Short answer: PrivateLink gives you simpler network isolation and avoids TGW route table complexity, but per-AZ costs scale with endpoints. TGW peering uses your existing backbone so cross-account routing can be cheaper for egress within the same org, but inter-region data transfer is charged by the cloud provider. We'll include cost examples for a two-region replication scenario.
[06:41] Jared Liu: For benchmarks, what data can we expect? We need p99 latency, token throughput, and tokens/sec per GPU estimates for your recommended model sizes.
[06:50] Omar Salazar: We'll run a short benchmark in our staging with the model you mentioned (redwood-7b-equivalent) and provide p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec metrics. Expect p99 in-region token latency to be <200ms on typical shapes for small models; larger models vary. We'll also include KV cache hit rate expectations when prefix-caching is enabled.
[07:08] Priya Nair: Can logs include full request context? We might need to avoid storing raw PII in logs for privacy regs.
[07:14] Maya Chen: Logs can be redacted at the point of export. We support field-level redaction and policy-based retention. For PII, you can set redaction rules — or we can route raw logs to an isolated bucket that your security team controls.
[07:26] Marco Ruiz: Any hard blockers you anticipate for our topology? Our TGW is used heavily, and we have strict IP ranges; we're concerned about IP overlap with Redwood's managed subnets.
[07:34] Omar Salazar: We avoid overlap by working with your team to allocate non-conflicting CIDR blocks. For Private deployments in your VPC, that's under your control. For PrivateLink we map to ENI IPs inside your VPC so no overlap issues. We'll need your CIDR sheet.
[07:46] Maya Chen: Marco, if you can send us the CIDR ranges and a diagram of TGW attachments, Omar and I will do an initial top-level design.
[07:53] Marco Ruiz: Will do.
[07:55] Jared Liu: Also, can you share a sample Terraform module or CloudFormation for how the Private endpoints and IAM roles look? That will speed internal review.
[08:03] Maya Chen: Yes, we have Terraform modules and a quickstart repo. I'll include links.
[08:07] Priya Nair: One operational question: how do you handle model updates/rollouts? We need canarying and an ability to rollback fast in case of regression.
[08:14] Omar Salazar: We support canary rollouts and A/B testing with traffic split rules at the routing layer. Private deployments can be managed by your CI/CD to trigger rollouts; we recommend a small canary pool with automated quality checks using Redwood Optimize eval hooks.
[08:26] Marco Ruiz: Great. Any changes that require subnet reconfiguration or downtime?
[08:29] Omar Salazar: Most ops are rolling; we can avoid downtime with blue-green or canary patterns. Network changes like adding endpoints or TGW attachments will require routing updates but we can coordinate maintenance windows.
[08:39] Maya Chen: Ok, to recap next steps: we'll share runbook, port matrix, Terraform quickstart, security pack, and a pricing sketch. Solaris will send CIDR ranges and a rough traffic profile. Omar will provision a short benchmark harness and invite Solaris to run tests in eu-west-1 and us-east-1.
[08:57] Marco Ruiz: Sounds good. Two small asks: include a sample Transit Gateway route table config and an example of PrivateLink NLB setup per AZ.
[09:05] Maya Chen: We'll include those in the runbook.
[09:08] Jared Liu: Thanks everyone.
[09:10] Priya Nair: Thanks.
[09:11] Maya Chen: Appreciate it, we'll follow up by EOD tomorrow with the docs.
